newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel sets PLO talks, vows new Jerusalem policy.
newsitem.headline: Israel sets PLO talks, vows new Jerusalem policy.

text.p: Israel set a high-level meeting with the Palestinians in the face of a seven-week-old peace deadlock on Sunday while promising a more even-handed policy with Arabs and Jews in Jerusalem.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat agreed to meet Israeli President Ezer Weizman at their border at 1500 GMT on Tuesday.

"I hope ideas will come up in this meeting that will help to rescue this process, treating at the roots the problems which brought about the present deep crisis," Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi told Israel Radio.

Weizman's job is largely ceremonial but he was an architect of Israel's 1979 peace with Egypt and has in the past smoothed relations made rocky since right-winger Benjamin Netanyahu became prime minister a year ago.

U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross arrives in the Middle East this week hoping to revive talks stalled since Israel broke ground for a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem and a Palestinian killed three Israeli women and himself in a Tel Aviv cafe blast.

Netanyahu's communications chief announced meanwhile that Israel would halt an 18-month-old policy in Arab East Jerusalem that had angered Palestinians, human rights groups and Israel's closest ally the United States.
Adviser David Bar-Illan said Netanyahu would stop revoking the residency of Palestinians who leave East Jerusalem, which Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed.

"The residents are not exactly immigrants but people who were born here and whose roots are deep in the city and we would like to remove what seems to be a very irritating bureaucratic procedure," he told Reuters.
Bar-Illan insisted an Israeli policy change had been in the works for months and was prompted neither by a U.S. complaint nor a search for goodwill gestures ahead of Ross's visit.
"I don't think it is anything that has to do with politics...We are trying to make the quality of life in Jerusalem as good as possible for everyone," he said.

Most of East Jerusalem's 160,000 residents reject Israeli citizenship. But Bar-Illan said Israel was willing to do what no other country would and grant them residency simply because of the inconvenience and bitter feelings the policy had created.

He said Israel would within two weeks start work on a government-subsidised housing project for Arabs near the new 6,500-unit Har Homa settlement for Jews which prompted Palestinians to freeze peace moves in March.

He said the Arab project -- made up of a "very substantial number of units" on top of 3,015 new private units already promised -- was meant to build confidence, "to show Arab residents we are looking after them as much as we are the Jewish residents," but he acknowledged difficulties getting Palestinians to go along.

"The major problem is that they don't want to admit Israel's sovereignty by collaborating with Israel," he said. Whereas Israel regards East Jerusalem as part of its indivisible capital, Palestinians view it as the capital of a future state.
Palestinian cabinet minister Hanan Ashrawi, reacting to Bar-Illan's proposals, told Reuters: "Israel tries to portray the cessation of its violations as concessions."

But she added: "These steps don't deal with the real issues. The basic issues are the status of Jerusalem and Israel should not take unilateral steps that prejudge the outcome of negotiations on Jerusalem, and the issue of land itself."

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy met shuttling European Middle East peace envoy Miguel Angel Moratinos who, despite Israeli headlines warning of Syrian preparations for war, told reporters: "What I heard in Damascus was the drum of peace."
